label: in the time of the long voyages
note: Settlement and the centuries of two-way voyaging to Kahiki. Radiocarbon models put the first settlement between about 940 and 1290; the traditions of Pāʻao, Moʻikeha and Laʻamaikahiki follow, and after Laʻa the traditions record no more voyages south. Coastal hamlets and the first loʻi in the windward valleys; the land mostly forest.

label: in the time of Māʻilikūkahi
note: Reign-indexed. Fornander's genealogies, at thirty years a generation, put Māʻilikūkahi in the 1400s; shorter generations bring him nearer 1500. The range brackets both. Each island has its own chiefs; Hāna still stands apart from the rest of Maui.

label: in the time of ʻUmi and Piʻilani
note: Reign-indexed. Fornander's reckoning puts ʻUmi's death about 1521–1526; Kirch's coral dates put the consolidation of Maui under Piʻilani and Kiha, ʻUmi's in-laws and allies, between about 1550 and 1700. The range brackets both. Hawaiʻi and Maui each united; field systems spreading on the leeward slopes.

label: in the time of Alapaʻinui
note: Alapaʻinui rules Hawaiʻi until his death in 1754 and carries war to Molokaʻi, Maui and Oʻahu; Fornander's dates for these wars are estimates.

label: in the time of Kalaniʻōpuʻu and Kahekili
note: Hawaiʻi holds Hāna from about 1759 and wars on Maui; Oʻahu holds Molokaʻi. Cook arrives in 1778.

label: in the time of Kahekili and the rise of Kamehameha
note: After Mokuʻōhai (1782) Hawaiʻi Island is split three ways; Kahekili of Maui takes Oʻahu and Molokaʻi in 1783. First guns, first cattle.

label: in the time of Kamehameha
note: From Nuʻuanu (1795) Kamehameha rules every island but Kauaʻi, which comes to him by agreement in 1810. Sandalwood cutting begins; the ʻōkuʻu of 1804.

label: in the time of Kaʻahumanu
note: The kapu system falls in 1819 and the missionaries arrive in 1820. Kaʻahumanu governs as kuhina nui; sandalwood, whaling ports.

label: in the time of Kauikeaouli, Kamehameha III
note: A constitutional kingdom: whaling at its height, the first plantation, the 1843 cession and restoration, the Māhele and the Kuleana Act, measles and smallpox.

label: in the time of Alexander Liholiho and Lota Kapuāiwa
note: Kamehameha IV and V. Kalaupapa from 1866. The population keeps falling; sugar grows.

label: in the time of Kalākaua
note: Lunalilo's short reign, then Kalākaua. Ditches carry the windward streams to the cane; the 1887 constitution shifts power to the planters.

label: in the time of Liliʻuokalani, and after
note: The Queen's reign from 1891, the overthrow of 1893, the Republic from 1894, annexation in 1898.

label: now
note: The coda, 1970 to the present: plantations closing, suburbs, and the return of loʻi, fishponds and voyaging. The only era whose people can be asked.
